## The question

**In one or two short paragraphs, introduce the setting, audience, focused research question, data source, observational unit, response, important predictors, and one important data limitation. Lead with what makes the question worth answering.**

AI may make the study process more efficient. However, not all forms of AI usage are as effective. Comparing unassisted test scores across AI groups can help math instructors make better decisions about how to use AI in class. We obtained the AI Learning dataset from[Carnegie Mellon Statistics & Data Science Data Repository](https://cmustatistics.github.io/data-repository/technology/ai-learning.html). This study uses data from Turkish high school students from grades 9 to 11. Students did practice problems with three different sources, including standard sources such as their notebooks and textbooks, GPT Base, and GPT Tutor. GPT Base offered general AI help, while GPT Tutor could provide students with hints without giving the solution directly. We only use the test scores in session one and from non-honors classes. The primary research question is how different uses of AI are associated with unassisted math test scores, after accounting for previous GPA and grade level. The observational unit is an individual high school student. The response is a student's unassisted math test decimal score (ranging from 0.00 to 1.00). Important predictors include AI use group, previous GPA, and grade level. Since we only use data from session 1, we only study students' immediate performance and cannot track their long-term performance.

## What the baseline shows

**Describe and justify a simple course-based baseline regression model. Interpret the result that best establishes the rest of the story, including its direction, magnitude, scale, and uncertainty. Explain one limitation or unresolved pattern that motivates deeper analysis.**

```{r}
# Load packages and data, document preparation, and fit the baseline.
library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)
library(car)
library(broom)
library(car)
library(bestglm)
learning_orig <- read.csv(
  "https://cmustatistics.github.io/data-repository/data/ai-learning.csv",
  check.names = FALSE
)

learning <- subset(learning_orig, Session == 1 & Honors == 0)

learning$`Treatment arm` <- factor(learning$`Treatment arm`)
learning$`Treatment arm` <- relevel(learning$`Treatment arm`, ref = "control")

baseline <- lm(Part3Tot ~ `Treatment arm` + gpa_prev + factor(Year), data = learning)

summary(baseline)

confint(baseline)
```

```{r}
# Show a primary figure or table only if it helps answer the question.
# <your code here>
ggplot(
  learning,
  aes(x = factor(Year), y = Part3Tot, color = `Treatment arm`, group =`Treatment arm`)) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", size = 3) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "line", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Grade level", y = "Mean Session 1 unassisted exam score",color = "AI group") +
  theme_minimal()
```

Fitted Baseline Model:

$$
\widehat{Part3Tot_i}=-1.738148+0.052384I(Teatment arm_i=augmented)-0.005518 I(Treatmentarm_i=vanilla)+ 1.518148 gpaprev_i+ 0.023248I(Year_i=10) + 0.197296 (Year_i=11)
$$

We modeled unassisted math score (Part3Tot) (0-1) using AI group (control, augmented = GPT Tutor, vanilla = GPT Base), previous GPA, and categorical grade level). Control and grade 9 are the reference groups. Holding GPA and previous GPA constant, students using GPT Tutor score, on average, 4.4839 percentage points higher (95% CI: \[0.67, 8.30\] percentage points) and students who use GPT Base score, on average, 0.6391 percentage points lower (95% CI: \[−4.64, 3.36\] percentage points) on the unassisted math test than students in the control group. These intervals does not account for unequal variance or spatial correlation.

The interaction plot suggests some interaction in this model. The mean of the GPT Base group is lower than other two groups in grades 9 and 11, while it is higher than the mean of the other two groups in grade 10.

The diagnostic plots showed that linearity and normality assumptions are generally met but suggest unequal variance. Students from the same classes may also have correlated residuals. We need to interpret the t- and F-test and two intervals with caution.

### How interaction is presented in the model

**Present one method and its most useful evidence.**

```{r}
# Analysis code for this part.
ai_learning_inx <- lm(Part3Tot ~  gpa_prev + `Treatment arm` * factor(Year), data = learning)
summary(ai_learning_inx)
anova(baseline,ai_learning_inx)
```

| Grade | Comparison          | Estimated difference (percentage points) | 95% CI |
|---------------|---------------|----------------------------|---------------|
| 9     | GPT Tutor − Control | 0.03148                                  |        |
| 9     | GPT Base - Control  | -0.05183                                 |        |
| 10    | GPT Tutor − Control |                                          |        |
| 10    | GPT Base - Control  |                                          |        |
| 11    | GPT Tutor − Control |                                          |        |
| 11    | GPT Base - Control  |                                          |        |

We add AI-group:grade level interaction to the model to allow differences in scores of AI-use groups to be different across grade levels.
